title: Design staged disaster recovery exercises: decision comparison 1
teachingQuestion: Given a recovery claim, which test form can produce the needed evidence without exceeding the authorized disruption?
focalInsight: Form selection, production impact, evidence, stop authority, and exercise-status communication.
caption: Compare meaning, decision conditions, and failures. These concise distinctions are paired with the worked examples in the teaching unit.

nodes.label: Drp Test
nodes.definition: A planned, authorized exercise of the disaster-recovery plan or capability, not a review of its existence.
nodes.decision: Choose a test only after naming the recovery claim, systems, participants, safety limits, and acceptance evidence.
nodes.failureExample: Calling a document review a DRP test leaves the failover path unproved.
nodes.detail: A planned, authorized exercise of the disaster-recovery plan or capability, not a review of its existence.

nodes.label: Test Objective
nodes.definition: The precise capability or decision the exercise is intended to prove, such as alternate-site processing or escalation timing.
nodes.decision: Write one observable objective before choosing form; reject vague objectives such as “test DR.”
nodes.failureExample: An undefined objective lets a team declare success although no recovery requirement was measured.
nodes.detail: The precise capability or decision the exercise is intended to prove, such as alternate-site processing or escalation timing.

nodes.label: Test Scope
nodes.definition: The bounded people, services, dependencies, locations, injects, and time window included in an exercise.
nodes.decision: Include dependencies needed to support the objective and explicitly exclude what must remain protected.
nodes.failureExample: A test of an application without identity, keys, or network dependencies falsely suggests recoverability.
nodes.detail: The bounded people, services, dependencies, locations, injects, and time window included in an exercise.

nodes.label: Read Through
nodes.definition: A participant-led reading of the plan to check comprehension, contacts, sequencing, and obvious contradictions without operating systems.
nodes.decision: Use first when plans are new or changed and the needed evidence is plan logic, not technical recovery.
nodes.failureExample: A read-through cannot prove that an alternate site, backup, or interface will operate.
nodes.detail: A participant-led reading of the plan to check comprehension, contacts, sequencing, and obvious contradictions without operating systems.

nodes.label: Tabletop
nodes.definition: A moderated discussion in which DR-role holders respond verbally to a disruptive scenario and decisions.
nodes.decision: Use to expose role, escalation, communication, and policy conflicts with no production action.
nodes.failureExample: Treating a tabletop as a technical failover test hides broken automation or inaccessible backups.
nodes.detail: A moderated discussion in which DR-role holders respond verbally to a disruptive scenario and decisions.

nodes.label: Walkthrough
nodes.definition: A step-by-step rehearsal in which participants trace assigned procedures and handoffs through a scenario.
nodes.decision: Use when the plan sequence or a cross-team handoff needs rehearsal before a live capability test.
nodes.failureExample: Skipping a handoff in a walkthrough can leave an unowned restoration decision undiscovered.
nodes.detail: A step-by-step rehearsal in which participants trace assigned procedures and handoffs through a scenario.

nodes.label: Simulation
nodes.definition: An exercise using realistic scenario injects to observe decisions, coordination, and response behavior without treating it as an actual outage.
nodes.decision: Use when uncertainty, timed choices, and communications must be stressed safely.
nodes.failureExample: A simulation that announces injects in advance cannot reveal delayed escalation or conflicting authority.
nodes.detail: An exercise using realistic scenario injects to observe decisions, coordination, and response behavior without treating it as an actual outage.

nodes.label: Parallel Test
nodes.definition: A test that operates recovery/alternate capability while normal production remains available.
nodes.decision: Use when evidence must show alternate operations work but service disruption is unacceptable; authorize resources and data protections.
nodes.failureExample: Running parallel work with unsanitized production data or no reconciliation can create a confidentiality or integrity incident.
nodes.detail: A test that operates recovery/alternate capability while normal production remains available.

nodes.label: Full Interruption
nodes.definition: A scripted exercise that transfers or stops normal operations across the organization to mimic a real contingency.
nodes.decision: Authorize only when the assurance need justifies maximum disruption and rollback, communications, and safety controls are ready.
nodes.failureExample: An ungoverned full interruption can cause real availability loss or confuse incident responders.
nodes.detail: A scripted exercise that transfers or stops normal operations across the organization to mimic a real contingency.

learningContract.teachingQuestion: Given a recovery claim, which test form can produce the needed evidence without exceeding the authorized disruption?
learningContract.misconception: A tabletop proves that recovery systems work, and a completed exercise is automatically a pass.
learningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
learningContract.focalInsight: Form selection, production impact, evidence, stop authority, and exercise-status communication.
learningContract.intentionalOmissions: Do not assign universal test frequency, RTO/RPO, or regulatory notification triggers.
learningContract.retrievalPrompt: A hospital must prove its alternate site can process real work while production continues. Which form, evidence, and safety boundary fit?
